passage: On the auto ride home from school in Kochi, Seema pressed close to her best friend Jomon. "Promise you won't tell?" Jomon nodded hard. "Lekha's aunty came to school, crying. I think her parents are fighting. Maybe they're even going to separate." Seema had only seen the aunty's red eyes. The fighting part just slipped out, and it made the story sound bigger. Jomon's mouth fell open. "Really?" "Really," Seema said, and somehow, saying it the second time, it sounded like something she had seen herself. At home, while she ate her banana chips, she told her little brother the same thing, with the word "separate" said even more surely.

qa.q: What did Seema actually see at school?
qa.a: She had only seen the aunty's red eyes.

qa.q: How can you tell Seema was starting to believe her own guess?
qa.a: Saying it a second time made it sound like something she had seen herself, and she repeated "separate" even more surely to her brother.

qa.q: What could Seema do to stop the story growing?
qa.a: She could tell Jomon that she only saw red eyes and guessed the rest, and stop repeating it.

qa.q: How might Jomon see the story now?
qa.a: Jomon probably believes it is true because Seema said "really" so confidently, and may pass it on as fact.

grounding: It shows a child retelling news to her best friend, adding a guessed detail that sounds truer each time it is told.

passage:
"Arnab, come here, I have to tell you something," Gopika whispered, pulling him behind the living room curtain.
"What?"
"You know Sudha from our class? She was crying in the corridor today."
"So?"
"So... I think she failed the maths test. Her mother was called to school."
"You saw her mother?"
"I... I think so. A lady in a blue sari."
Arnab's eyes went wide. "Failed? Sudha? She's so good at maths!"
"That's why it's so shocking," Gopika said, and she felt a little thrill. "And the lady was really angry."
"Gopika! Arnab! Homework!" Mummy called from the kitchen.
Gopika hopped out. Her story had grown, and now she almost believed it herself.

qa.q: What colour sari was the lady wearing?
qa.a: The lady was wearing a blue sari.

qa.q: What did Gopika feel when Arnab looked shocked?
qa.a: She felt a little thrill, enjoying how interesting her story had become. 🤔

qa.q: What could Gopika notice about her story, and what could she do?
qa.a: She could notice that the failed test and the angry lady were her guesses, not things she saw, and tell Arnab she isn't sure.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel if the story reaches her class?
qa.a: She would feel confused and hurt, being talked about for failing a test she may not have failed at all.

grounding: It illustrates a child telling her best friend a story and adding guessed details that start to feel true to her.

passage:
Monday. Urmila saw Deepa's mother arrive at school in the middle of maths and take Deepa home early. Deepa was crying.

Tuesday. On the walk home, Urmila told her best friend Saurabh. "Deepa's mother took her home crying." Saurabh didn't look very interested, so she added, "I think her parents are getting divorced. Her mother looked really angry."

She hadn't seen an angry face. She had only seen Deepa crying. But saying it made the story better, and Saurabh's eyes went wide.

Thursday. Urmila told the story again to her cousin. This time she said, "Her parents are getting divorced," without the "I think." It sounded true now. She almost believed she'd seen the angry face herself.

Friday. Deepa came back to school. Her grandmother had been in hospital. That was all.

qa.q: Why had Deepa actually gone home early?
qa.a: Her grandmother had been in hospital.

qa.q: Why did Urmila add the detail about the divorce?
qa.a: Saurabh didn't look very interested, and she wanted the story to be more exciting; she enjoyed his eyes going wide.

qa.q: What could Urmila have done differently?
qa.a: Say only what she saw, Deepa leaving crying, or not share it at all, instead of adding a guess.

qa.q: How might Deepa feel if she heard the divorce story?
qa.a: She would probably feel hurt and confused, since it wasn't true and she was already worried about her grandmother.

grounding: Over a week Urmila retells what she saw to her best friend, adding a guessed detail that sounds truer each time she tells it.

passage:
Thomas, a story about your friend got bigger as it went round, you said? Let your Pema aunty tell you what I did as a girl in Darjeeling.

One morning our neighbour's daughter, Dolkar, came to school with a bandage on her hand. That was all I saw.

I told my best friend, Nima. A bandage wasn't exciting, so I said, "I think she got into a fight with the milkman's boy." Nima gasped, and I loved it.

A week later, the story was that Dolkar fought boys daily and had been sent away from her old school. Even I started to believe it.

Then Dolkar's mother came to our house, very upset. Dolkar had cut her hand on a tin while cooking.

The turning point, Thomas, was that little "I think." There I chose excitement over truth.

qa.q: How had Dolkar actually hurt her hand?
qa.a: She cut her hand on a tin while cooking.

qa.q: Why did young Pema add the detail about Dolkar's brother?
qa.a: She wanted the story to be exciting and enjoyed Nima's gasp.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Pema's story?
qa.a: The moment she added "I think she got into a fight with the milkman's boy," choosing excitement over the truth.

qa.q: How did Dolkar's mother feel when she came to the house?
qa.a: She was very upset, probably hurt and angry that a false story about her family had spread.

grounding: Pema aunty recalls adding a guessed detail to what she saw when telling her best friend, and how the guess grew and sounded truer with each retelling.

passage:
It was raining so hard that the whole school was kept indoors for lunch. Sangeeta and Pallavi sat in a corner of the hall.

"Guess what," Sangeeta whispered. "I saw Megha's father come to school today. He was talking to Ma'am for a long time."

Pallavi shrugged. "So?"

Sangeeta wanted her to be excited. So she added, "He looked really angry. Megha must have done something bad. Maybe she stole something."

She had not seen an angry face. The father had looked tired, if anything.

Pallavi's eyes widened. "Stole? What?"

"I don't know. Something big, probably."

By the end of lunch, Sangeeta had half convinced herself it was true. It sounded so real when she said it.

After the bell, Megha walked past, head down. Sangeeta suddenly didn't feel excited at all.

qa.q: Why was the whole school kept indoors for lunch?
qa.a: It was raining so hard.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta feel when Megha walks past after the bell?
qa.a: She no longer feels excited; she feels uneasy and guilty about the story she made bigger.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do now?
qa.a: Tell Pallavi that she made up the stealing part, so the guess doesn't keep spreading as if it were true.

qa.q: What might Megha be feeling as she walks past with her head down?
qa.a: She may be sad or worried about whatever brought her father to school, unaware of the rumour.

grounding: On a rainy indoor lunch, Sangeeta tells her best friend what she saw and adds a guess to make it exciting, half believing it herself.

passage:
During the lunch break at their Bhopal school, Indu pulled Abhinav behind the water cooler. "You're my best friend, so I'll tell only you," she said. "Yesterday I saw Shabnam's mother shouting at her near the gate."
That part was true. Indu had seen a woman speaking loudly, and Shabnam staring at her shoes.
"And," Indu went on, lowering her voice, "I think she's going to be sent to another school."
Abhinav's eyes went round. "Really?"
"Really," said Indu. As she said it, it sounded real even to her. Nobody had mentioned another school. But the story felt better with that part in, and Abhinav was listening so hard.

qa.q: Where did Indu pull Abhinav during the lunch break?
qa.a: She pulled him behind the water cooler.

qa.q: Why did Indu add the part about another school?
qa.a: She enjoyed feeling important and wanted the story to sound more exciting, and the guess began to feel true even to her.

qa.q: What could Indu do before adding to a story next time?
qa.a: She could ask herself, 'Did I see this or am I guessing?' and leave out anything she only imagined, or not share it at all.

qa.q: How might Shabnam feel if she heard this version of the story?
qa.a: Shabnam would likely feel hurt and embarrassed, since the story adds something that never happened.

grounding: Shows a child telling her best friend what she saw and adding a guessed detail that soon sounds true.
